summary: This informational document registers media types for several library and metadata XML formats: MODS, MADS, METS, MARCXML, and the SRU response format. With registered types, systems can label such documents correctly when moving them over protocols like HTTP and email.

eli5.summary: Libraries have special kinds of catalog cards written as computer files. This document gives those file kinds official names so computers can tell them apart.

subtitle: Register official names for library metadata XML formats.

tldr.problem: Libraries and archives manage data in several XML formats (MODS, MADS, METS, MARCXML, SRU), but these had no registered MIME media types, so systems could not correctly label them when transmitting over HTTP or email.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers five media types with IANA: one each for MODS, MADS, METS, MARCXML, and SRU response format, all as XML subtypes of the application type.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now explicitly declare the format of library metadata documents and search results, enabling proper parsing and handling across networks.

today: RFC 6207 remains current as the authoritative registration of MIME media types for these five library metadata formats. All five types are registered with IANA and widely used in digital library systems, institutional repositories, and search services.

sections.title: Library Metadata Standards
sections.content:
The Library of Congress maintains several XML schemas for describing and organizing information: MODS (Metadata Object Description Schema) for bibliographic data, MADS (Metadata Authority Description Schema) for authority records about people, organizations, and subjects, METS (Metadata Encoding and Transmission Standard) for descriptive and structural metadata, MARCXML (the XML representation of MARC21 cataloging records), and SRU (Search/Retrieve via URL) response format. These are widely used by libraries, archives, and digital repositories.

Without registered media types, systems had no standard way to label these documents when sending them over HTTP, email, or other protocols. This RFC registers each one with IANA so that applications can declare and recognize the format unambiguously.
sections.eli5: Libraries have different ways to write down what books and records they have. This document says 'here is the official name for each kind of list'.

sections.title: The Five Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers five media types, all with charset parameter support (following application/xml as defined in RFC 3023):

application/mods+xml: Describes bibliographic objects with meaningful element names (such as title, author, publisher) rather than the coded abbreviations used in MARC. MODS is commonly used in digital library applications.

application/mads+xml: Records authority data for names, subjects, geographic locations, and genres, typically used alongside MODS for consistent subject indexing.

application/mets+xml: Encodes descriptive, administrative, and structural metadata for digital objects, combining the roles of multiple schemas.

application/marcxml+xml: The direct XML serialization of MARC21 records, preserving the coded fields of the original MARC format but allowing XML processing.

application/sru+xml: The default response format for the SRU search protocol, used in SRU 2.0 and later where clients can request alternative formats.
sections.eli5: MODS is like a detailed book catalog. MADS holds information about authors and subjects. METS is a container for all kinds of metadata. MARCXML is the same thing as the old MARC format but written in a modern way. SRU is the format for search results from a library server.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
Each registration includes encoding considerations (identical to those of application/xml), file extensions (.mods, .mads, .mets, .marcxml, .sru), and contact information for further questions. Applications using these media types include MODS-conformant toolkits, digital library platforms, and authority management systems.

The RFC notes that XML itself carries inherent security risks. XML entities can reference external resources, and parsing untrusted XML can lead to denial-of-service attacks. Implementations MUST carefully validate XML and, where appropriate, disable external entity resolution. The formats themselves do not contain executable code, but recipients should apply the same caution they would to any XML document.
sections.eli5: Once a program knows what kind of file it is receiving, it can read it safely, but it should never trust that the file is what it claims to be.

sections.title: Current Status and Use
sections.content:
All five media types are registered with IANA and in use across the library and information retrieval community. MODS and MARCXML are particularly widespread in digital library systems. METS is used by many institutional repositories and digitization projects. MADS is standard for authority control. SRU is used by Z39.50 servers and library search systems, with SRU 2.0 enabling content negotiation that relies on these media types.

The RFC is an Informational standards-track publication from the IETF and remains current as these formats continue to be the primary XML standards for library metadata.
sections.eli5: Libraries around the world use these formats to organize and share their catalogs.
